rows.evidence: Q1: Section 2.6 and Fig. 1 report new, previously unpublished bean-yield data (n = 10 <U+00B1> SE, three harvests 2013<U+2013>2015) from the authors' FACE trial on unirrigated C. arabica cv. Catua<U+00ED> in Brazil, described as 'this study'.
rows.notes: The paper is essentially a review of coffee responses to elevated CO2 and heat, with one new dataset (FACE yields). It contains no result of its own on drip or sensor-based irrigation; the only own experiment is rain-fed/unirrigated and compares elevated vs ambient CO2. Irrigation is mentioned only in passing (intensive systems 'including irrigation' may benefit more from CO2; Verhage et al. assumption that irrigation use remains the same), which is discussion, not a finding. Nothing supports drip irrigation as a climate-risk/drought adaptation measure.

rows.evidence: Q1: Section 2.6 and Fig. 1 report the authors' own FACE yield data (three harvests, n = 10 <U+00B1> SE) for unirrigated C. arabica in Brazil.
rows.notes: No own result on micro-irrigation or rainwater harvesting; the study's own evidence concerns elevated atmospheric CO2 effects on photosynthesis, yield, heat tolerance and bean quality in coffee. Irrigation appears only as a passing remark in the discussion (intensive systems including irrigation may show clearer CO2 benefits), not as a tested technology. The claim about integrating rainwater harvesting and micro-irrigation as drought adaptation is not supported by anything in this paper.
